newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - British tribunal investigates child abuse claims.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - British tribunal investigates child abuse claims.

text.p: Shackled to a policeman and with tears streaming down his face, the burly prisoner describes in horrific detail the abuse he endured during six years in a north Wales children's home.
"Late that night they both came to me and I was molested in a pretty bad way by both of them," the 32-year-old witness, aged 10 at the time of the assault, told the hushed tribunal.
"I don't know whose hands were doing what," he added, recalling his time at the Bryn Allen private children's home.
Bryn Allen is one of 39 state and private children's homes that operated in two Welsh counties from 1974 to 1996 and are now the focus of Britain's largest child abuse investigation.
More than 650 alleged victims have filed complaints against 85 employees of the homes. Since the tribunal began in this small town in January 160 people have testified.

Such is the scale of the allegations, the tribunal is expected to last until the end of the year hearing testimony from alleged victims, their accused abusers and social workers and employees in charge of supervising the homes.
By the time it is over it is estimated it will have cost more than eight million pounds ($13 million).
Bryn Allen's owner, John Alyn, is serving a six-year prison sentence following a conviction in 1995 for six offences of indecent assault on boys in his care.
His home and Bryn Estyn, where three former employees, including deputy head Peter Howarth, were jailed for sex abuse offences, were the source of the majority of complaints.
The children, almost all boys and some as young as eight, were sent to the homes after being orphaned, abandoned or for minor criminal offences.

Instead of a safe haven, they claim they lived in terror of night-time visits, of being gang raped in toilets, of public humilation at all-male parties, of physical assaults and pornographic photo sessions.

"I can remember that once or twice a week after going to the dormitories to go to bed, a male member of staff would come to the door and call out one of the boys who would get up and leave," said one former Bryn Estyn resident in a statement.
"They were normally gone for half an hour to an hour. When they returned they went back into bed and I often heard them sobbing. I never asked what happened because I was afraid," he added.
Howarth, who was due to testify at the tribunal, was jailed for 10 years in 1993 for sexual offences, including masturbation, oral sex and buggery, against seven boys. He died in prison in April.

For many of the boys Alyn and Howarth, although their alleged abusers, were like father figures and gave some of them the only attention they ever had. They lavished their favourites with expensive gifts, holidays and promises of home leave in return for abusing them.
"I never thought of it as wrong," sobbed one witness. "He led me to believe it was OK."
SCARRED FOR LIFE
The enormity of what the men say they have experienced has scarred many for life.
Some went on to criminal careers and have fied while handcuffed to their police guards. Many have broken down on the witness stand and some did not live to tell their story.
"For too many, it seems, the consequences have been too hard to bear and suicide has seemed the only way out," said lawyer Gerard Elias in his opening statement to the tribunal.
"At least 10 former children in care in north Wales who have alleged abuse are now dead -- most of those are known to have taken their own lives," he added.
The tribunal is trying to determine what happened and why, and if it happened, what can be done to stop similar abuse in the future.
INVESTIGATION INTO POSSIBLE PAEDOPHILE RING
Because the claims are so widespread and cover a 20-year period, the investigation is also looking into the possibility that a paedophile ring operated in the north Wales care system.

"There can be little doubt that most or all of the most serious sexual abusers knew each other. The homes presented attractive targets to them. Children in care form a particularly vulnerable class," said Elias.

For many of the men it is the first time they have talked about what they experienced. Most said there was no one they could have confided in and they would have risked even worse treatment if they had complained.
A few said they were rented out as male prostitutes to prominent Britons, a few of whom have been named during the tribunal, along with six police officers.

Elias has also suggested that local government councils may have deliberately stymied earlier investigations after an insurance company advised in a letter that every inquiry was a "dress rehearsal for claimants and a further incentive to the bandwagon syndrome."
Police sent files to the government prosecution service three times and a council also investigated the allegations but nothing was done.
It wasn't until Alison Taylor, a former care worker who was fired after going to the police with the abuse complaints of a teenager, compiled a dossier of claims that something finally happened.
Her findings led to an independent investigation by child care experts and a 300-age report that concluded that widespread abuse had occurred.
Former prime minister John Major ordered the triubanl after a British newspaper published the report last summer. Fifteen police forces in Britain have also started child abuse investigations.
"We must start listening to children," one witness pleaded in a statement to the tribunal.
"Do not ignore them in the way we have ignored them for many years. Listen to our children's cries. Listen to what they are saying and take action without delay."
The man, described as a star witness, vowed that he had told the truth but said he still felt guilty.
"I feel very guilty for the fact that I have not been able to tell you everything that went on and in some cases, is still going on."
Tribunal chairman Ronald Waterhouse, a former high court judge, is expected to produce his findings early next year.
